catalog_quote: Every vowel will have either a high pitch (tone) (which in word-final position is a falling pitch contour) or a low pitch accompanying it. The distribution of pitches is entirely unpredictable and phonemic; stress, which occurs in three degrees (primary, secondary, and unstressed) can be predicted most of the time from the position of the pitches. ... The rules for stress prediction are complex, and unexplained counterexamples exist. For primary stress, a hierarchy of priorities exists: in a given word, all high-pitched syllables will have primary stress; if no high pitches occur in the word, long vowels receive primary stress; if neither high pitch nor a long vowel occurs in the word, the last voiced vowel has primary stress—except that in two-vowel words with only short, low-pitched vowels, neither vowel is more strongly stressed than the other. ... sources.citation: Rood, David S. 1971. Wichita: An Unusual Phonology System. Colorado Research in Linguistics 1: R1-R24. Boulder: University of Colorado. DOI 10.25810/a3tf-4246 (open access, CU Scholar).
sources.quote: Prosodic system = phonemic high vs. non-high pitch plus a three-way vowel-length contrast; Garvin's 'phonemic primary stress' is reanalysed as high pitch (stress coincides with high-pitched syllables; all-low-pitch words show variable/indeterminate stress); secondary stress alternates on every second vowel in either direction. The explicit long-vowel clause of the 1996 hierarchy is not yet stated here.
sources.locator: sec. 1.1-1.2 (p. R2-R3: summary of Garvin 1950: 'a phoneme.. of primary stress placement'; 'Garvin is convinced of the phonemic, non-predictable status of primary stress. Secondary stress, however, is almost predictable, occurring usually on every second vowel in either direction from the primary stress'); sec. 2.2.2 'Pitch' (p. R12-R13: 'Garvin analyzed the distinction between high and low pitch as one of primary stress and then thought he heard primary stress in every word. His examples of variable stress are forms which have all low pitches.. in words with one or more high pitched syllables, Garvin (1950) always marked stress on the high pitches. His minimal pair for stress is really one for pitch'); fn. 5 (Garvin & Hill 1962 later recognized phonemic pitch as well).
sources.note: Open-access precursor; explicitly reanalyses Garvin's 'phonemic primary stress' as high pitch, which resolves the Garvin-1950-via-SPA-1979 partial disagreement recorded in the contra field.
